newsitem.title: USA: U.S. violent crime rate shows steep decline in 1995.
newsitem.headline: U.S. violent crime rate shows steep decline in 1995.

text.p: The U.S. violent crime rate plunged more than 12 percent in 1995 in the steepest drop since the survey of victims began 24 years ago, according to a Justice Department report released on Sunday.

The survey by the department's information-gathering Bureau of Justice Statistics found dramatic declines for violent crimes such as rapes, robberies and assaults, as well as for other offences, such as thefts and household burglaries.
The greatest decrease in violent offences last year took place in the nation's suburbs, followed by rural areas and the cities, which have been hit hard by crime, the report said.

It said the drop in crime was greater for white victims than for blacks. The only statistically significant change for blacks was a 24 percent drop in aggravated assaults. Crime victim rates for Hispanics showed no significant change.
President Bill Clinton hailed the new figures as a sign that his plan to fight crime was working.
"Now we must press forward. Fighting the scourge of juvenile crime and violence is my top law enforcement priority for the next four years," he said in a written statement.

Clinton urged Congress to pass "without delay" the Anti-Gang and Youth Violence Strategy Bill he sent to Capitol Hill in February. The measure declared war on gangs with new prosecutors and tougher penalties, prohibiting violent teenage criminals from purchasing handguns and providing resources to keep schools open late on weekends and in summer.

Preliminary figures on the drop in crime had been announced by Clinton in September during a campaign trip to Michigan. The new figures gave the final numbers for 1995 and showed the decline had been greater than previously thought.

"These statistics show that we can make a difference in our efforts to combat crime," Attorney General Janet Reno said in a statement. "We are moving in the right direction, but we must not let up our efforts to protect the public safety."
From the mid-1980s until the early 1990s, the U.S. crime rate soared, fuelled by more murders, drug-related violence and inner-city gangs.
Experts have attributed the recent declines in crime to various factors, including the ageing of the baby-boom generation past the prime years for committing crimes.
They also have cited better police strategies, improved crime prevention measures, tougher gun control laws and a dramatic increase in the number of criminals in U.S. prisons.
Among specific categories, the report found declines of 24 percent in aggravated assaults, 26 percent for personal thefts, 13 percent for burglaries and more than 8 percent for household thefts.
Motor vehicle theft was the only type of crime which did not register a significant decline last year.
The annual survey has been on interviews with about 100,000 people to determine if they have been a victim of crime.
Because the survey involved interviews with crime victims, it does not include murders. But separate FBI reports have shown a steady decline in murders over the past several years.
